claims.text: Lightweight high-entropy alloys can combine low density, mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Substituting heavier elements with low-density oxide-forming elements such as Al or Ti lowers or maintains low alloy density.
Substituted Al or Ti forms finely dispersed, stable nano-oxides at grain boundaries and within the alloy matrix.
The proposed starting alloy is a single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy containing both heavier and low-density oxide-forming elements.
The substituted reactive elements will internally oxidize during service.
Internal oxidation will produce nanoscale oxide dispersions.
The relevant oxide particles will be distributed both along grain boundaries and within the matrix.
Fine, stable oxide dispersions pin grain boundaries.
Fine, stable oxide dispersions impede dislocation motion and thereby reinforce the alloy.
Oxides act as barriers against corrosive attack.
Oxides act as barriers against high-temperature oxidative attack.
Relative to a baseline without light-element substitution, the modified alloy will have higher yield strength.
Relative to the baseline, the modified alloy will have higher tensile strength.
Relative to the baseline, the modified alloy will have a lower corrosion rate.
Relative to the baseline, the modified alloy will have improved high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Replacing heavier elements with Al or Ti will cause only a marginal density change relative to the baseline.
The mechanism will cease to operate in strongly reducing atmospheres that prevent oxide formation.
The mechanism will cease to provide the proposed benefits if the substituted elements form coarse detrimental precipitates rather than fine oxide dispersions.
Strength and corrosion or oxidation improvements depend on processing parameters, oxide size and distribution, and operating conditions.
A dense surface oxide film can reduce hydrogen uptake and provide corrosion resistance in a multicomponent FCC alloy.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis motivates replacing heavier elements with low-density elements as the basis for low density, but the prediction specifies only a marginal density change and does not clearly predict a density decrease relative to the heavier-element baseline.
